benchmark_kind: cost of running the same generated circuit under a malicious-security protocol instead of a passive one
scope_warning: Single host, one query, one repetition, on the smallest bundled fixture. All three parties ran on one machine, which does not instantiate the non-collusion assumption. This measures the cost of a protocol swap on one circuit shape; it does NOT make the system maliciously secure, because the owner-input and client-output boundaries remain unauthenticated. See what_this_does_NOT_establish below.
what_was_measured: The identical compiled program, identical private inputs, and identical three-party committee, executed once under MP-SPDZ Semi and once under MP-SPDZ MASCOT.

semi.note: This is the protocol every other benchmark in this directory uses.

mascot.note: Same corruption threshold as Semi: three parties, up to two corrupted. Only the adversary's behaviour changes, from passive to actively deviating.

fixture.note: The smallest available paged fixture was used because MASCOT's preprocessing cost made anything larger impractical to run here.

correctness.comparison: Both runs were decoded from the three per-server output logs and compared for exact JSON equality against evaluate_paged_cleartext.

what_this_establishes: The generated circuit compiles and executes correctly under a malicious-security protocol without modification: it uses no construct that requires passive security.
A concrete price for the upgrade on this circuit shape: about 31x wall-clock and about 155x communication on a single host with preprocessing included.
what_this_does_NOT_establish: This system is NOT maliciously secure end to end, and no such claim is made anywhere in this repository.

The owner-to-server input boundary is unauthenticated. Owners hand each server an additive share; nothing forces an owner to submit shares that reconstruct to a well-formed layout, and MASCOT does not check this because the check would have to happen outside the MPC. A malicious owner can therefore still corrupt results.
The server-to-client output boundary is unauthenticated. Each server prints its own output share; nothing stops a malicious server from releasing a wrong share, and the client cannot detect it.
No ideal functionality has been written and no simulation proof exists, for either protocol.
Single host, one query, one repetition. All three parties ran on one machine, which does not instantiate the non-collusion assumption.
MASCOT's abort guarantee is security-with-abort: a detected cheater halts the computation, it does not yield a correct answer.
reading: Malicious security of the three-party computation is available off the shelf and costs about two orders of magnitude in communication. Closing the remaining gap is not a protocol swap: it needs authenticated owner input (a commitment or MAC on each owner's shares, checked in-circuit) and authenticated output release, neither of which is implemented.
